summary: Describes the Finger protocol, a simple interface to a remote user information program. It is based on RFC 742 and makes minor corrections and clarifications to RFC 1194. It was replaced by RFC 1288.

eli5.summary: You knock on a computer's door and ask who is home. This is a cleaned-up version of the rules for asking.

questions: how does finger query forwarding work
subtitle: How to ask a remote computer who is logged in, and what it may tell you.

tldr.problem: People wanted a simple way to look up information about users on a remote host, but the original Finger description left the expected behaviour unclear and the protocol discloses sensitive data.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 79, sends a one-line ASCII query ending in CRLF, and the remote user information program (RUIP) returns a human-readable answer and closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: The memo clarifies the query forms and adds extensive security guidance. It was obsoleted by RFC 1288.

today: RFC 1196 is a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 742 and RFC 1194, and it was itself obsoleted by RFC 1288, which is the version to read.

sections.title: Intent and History
sections.content:
RFC 1196 describes the Finger User Information Protocol, a simple protocol giving an interface to a remote user information program (RUIP). It is based on RFC 742, the original Name/Finger description, and tries to clarify the expected communication between the two ends without invalidating existing implementations or adding unnecessary restrictions. It also corrects and clarifies in a minor way RFC 1194.

The memo is built around the behaviour of the BSD version, the most prevalent implementation at the time. Because that version offered few ways to tailor Finger to a site's security policy, the memo adds many security comments and recommendations. It uses the RFC 2119-style capitalised words MUST, SHOULD and MAY, and defines conditional and unconditional compliance.
sections.eli5: This is a tidier version of the old rules for asking who is home, with extra warnings about keeping people's information safe.

sections.title: Connection and Query Format
sections.content:
Finger runs over TCP, using TCP port 79 decimal (117 octal). The client opens a connection, sends a one-line query, the RUIP processes it, returns an answer and closes the connection normally. All data MUST be ASCII with no parity, and lines end in CRLF.

The query is defined as {Q1} ::= [{U}] [/W] {C} and {Q2} ::= [{U}]{H} [/W] {C}, where {U} is a username, {H} is one or more @hostname tokens and {C} is CRLF. Because {H} is recursive, there is no arbitrary limit on the number of hosts. An RUIP MUST accept the entire query specification. The query refers to the line the RUIP actually receives: if a user types finger user@host, the remote RUIP receives user followed by CRLF, which is a {Q1} query.
sections.eli5: You write a one-line note, maybe with a person's name on it, and hand it to the front desk at door number 79.

sections.title: What the Server Answers
sections.content:
A {C} query (an empty line) asks for a list of all online users. The RUIP MUST either answer or actively refuse. If it answers, it MUST give at least each user's full name, and the administrator SHOULD be able to add things such as terminal location, office location, phone number, job name and idle time.

A {U}{C} query asks for in-depth status on one user. The answer MUST include at least the full name, and if the user is logged in, at least as much as the {C} list gives. Optional extras include a user information file (often called a plan file) and running a user program; each SHOULD be switchable by the administrator. Names MUST include login names, and for an ambiguous name the administrator SHOULD choose whether all matches are returned. The /W token SHOULD at best signal more verbose output at the last RUIP, or at worst be ignored.

Output is written for people rather than programs, so it has no strict format. The memo also includes a light-hearted note that vending machines SHOULD answer a {C} request with the items available and should never eat requests or money.
sections.eli5: Asking with no name gets you a list of who is around. Asking with a name gets you more detail about that one person.

sections.title: Forwarding Queries Across Hosts
sections.content: A {Q2} query asks an RUIP to forward the query to another RUIP. An RUIP MUST either provide this service or actively refuse it. If it forwards, it works from the right-most host: given FOO@HOST1@HOST2, the RUIP on HOST2 opens its own Finger connection to HOST1 with the query FOO, returns whatever it receives, and closes the original connection only when the onward connection closes.
sections.eli5: It is like passing a note down a line of friends: each one hands it on to the next and brings the reply back.

sections.title: Security Guidance
sections.content:
The memo says Finger is one of the avenues for direct penetration, as the Morris worm pointed out, and should get as much security scrutiny as Telnet, FTP or SMTP. Finger discloses information about users that may be sensitive, so administrators should decide explicitly whether to run it and what to reveal.

Key recommendations: administrators SHOULD be able to turn {Q2} forwarding off, and the RECOMMENDED default is to refuse it; a refusal MUST return a message such as "Finger forwarding service denied". The same applies to refusing the {C} list ("Finger online user list denied"). Administrators SHOULD be able to choose exactly which pieces of information are returned, the minimum being the full name. User information files and user-run programs are dangerous, and implementations SHOULD allow logging of queries.

Clients SHOULD by default filter output down to printable characters (ASCII 32 through 126), tabs and CRLFs, to protect against terminal escape codes, with options to allow international or control characters.
sections.eli5: A front desk should not blurt out everything about everybody. The desk's boss should choose what it says, and visitors should not be tricked by sneaky messages.

references.text: Zimmerman, D., "The Finger User Information Protocol", RFC 1194, November 1990.
